title: Async cleanup helpers (GH#20554/#21997/#22415) share the parent pulse cgroup — KillMode=control-group kills them too when TimeoutStartSec fires
body:
## Description

The async background-cleanup pattern introduced by GH#20554 (worktree cleanup), GH#21997 (stash cleanup), and GH#22415 (remote-branch cleanup) detaches each job via `nohup "$helper" ... & disown $!` (`.agents/scripts/pulse-dispatch-preflight-lib.sh:98-131`) specifically so a slow cleanup pass cannot block the pulse cycle.

That detachment protects the helper from the *parent shell exiting normally*, but it does **not** move the helper into a new cgroup. The systemd user service `aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service` runs with `KillMode=control-group` and `TimeoutStartSec=1860`. When a cycle exceeds the timeout, systemd SIGKILLs the entire cgroup — including every `nohup`'d/`disown`'d async helper still running inside it. The three GH#20554/#21997/#22415 helpers therefore share fate with the parent cycle in exactly the scenario they were built to be independent of: a slow/hung cycle.

Net effect observed on this machine: `aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service` failed via `TimeoutStartSec` + SIGKILL **7 times between 10:42 and 14:50 CEST today** (~4 hours, one cycle roughly every 30 min, none completing). `~/Git/_worktrees` has accumulated 27-28 stale linked worktrees (~11 GB), most tied to branches that were never merged or to dispatch sessions whose owning PID is long dead, going back to 2026-07-17.

This is not an absolute "cleanup never runs" claim — it is a race. In this same session, one `cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh` invocation *did* complete successfully (removed 2 worktrees, logged at 2026-08-02T13:33:45Z) because it finished before its parent cycle's timeout fired. Other invocations, spawned under cycles that were later SIGKILLed, did not get a matching "Completed successfully" log line before the kill. Whether a given cycle's cleanup progress survives is therefore determined by an unmanaged race against the parent's `TimeoutStartSec`, not by the single-runner/cadence guard the helpers implement internally.

## Expected Behavior

An async job detached specifically to survive a slow/hung parent cycle (per GH#20554/#21997/#22415's own stated rationale) should not be killed when that parent cycle hits its timeout. It should run in its own cgroup/scope so `KillMode=control-group` on the parent service cannot reach it, and should be left to finish or be governed by its own independent timeout.

## Reproducer

**Symptom command**:

```
systemctl --user status aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service --no-pager -l
```

**Actual output** (captured 2026-08-02, ~15:32 CEST, while the service was 17+ min into a cycle):

```
● aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service - aidevops aidevops-supervisor-pulse
     Active: activating (start) since Sun 2026-08-02 15:14:46 CEST; 17min ago
   Main PID: 548925 (bash)
     CGroup: /user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service
             ├─548925 bash .../agents/scripts/pulse-wrapper.sh
             ├─620000 bash .../agents/scripts/cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh
             ├─889983 bash .../agents/scripts/pulse-wrapper.sh
             ├─908766 bash .../agents/scripts/pulse-wrapper.sh
             ├─908770 bash .../agents/scripts/gh api repos/Majowka/netbox-wg/issues/1419/timeline --paginate --slurp
             ├─915345 bash .../agents/scripts/cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh
             ├─915346 bash .../agents/scripts/cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh
             └─(git/awk/jq children)
```

Journal for the same service across the preceding ~4 hours (`journalctl --user -u aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service --since "10:40" --until "14:50"`) shows 7 occurrences of:

```
aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service: Failed with result 'signal'.  (or 'timeout')
aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service: Killing process <PID> (bash) with signal SIGKILL.
```

`~/.aidevops/logs/cleanup_worktrees.log` (52 MB, spans the same period) ends its most recent entries at:

```
[pulse-wrapper] Worktree cleanup total: 2 worktree(s) removed across all repos
[cleanup-worktrees-async] Completed successfully at 2026-08-02T13:33:45Z. last-run updated.
```

— confirmed by `~/.aidevops/logs/cleanup_worktrees.last-run` containing epoch `1785677625` = `2026-08-02T13:33:45Z`, matched against `date -u` at time of check (`2026-08-02T13:34:03Z`), i.e. the most recent successful completion was ~18s before this check — but no completion line appears for any of the cycles killed during the preceding 10:42-14:47 window in the same log.

**Expected output**: the async helper either finishes on its own schedule regardless of the parent cycle's fate, or fails/reports independently — never silently disappears because a sibling process (the parent pulse-wrapper.sh) exceeded a timeout that has nothing to do with the helper's own progress.

**Blocked command**: not a hang in the traditional sense — the child command that gets terminated mid-run is the detached helper itself, e.g. `bash .../agents/scripts/cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh` (observed live as PIDs 620000, 915345, 915346), shown nested directly under `aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service`'s own `CGroup:` in `systemctl --user status` output while the parent cycle was still inside its `TimeoutStartSec` window.

**Backend state**: `journalctl --user -u aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service` records, for each of the 7 timeout events between 10:42-14:50 CEST, explicit lines of the form `aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service: Killing process <PID> (bash) with signal SIGKILL.` immediately following `start operation timed out. Terminating.` — i.e. systemd's own log confirms it is killing every process in the cgroup, not just the tracked main PID. Cross-referenced against `~/.aidevops/logs/cleanup_worktrees.log` (52 MB) and `.last-run` (epoch `1785677625` = `2026-08-02T13:33:45Z`, checked at `2026-08-02T13:34:03Z`): the only "Completed successfully" line in the entire log corresponds to a helper invocation that finished ~18s before this check, i.e. it raced ahead of its parent's timeout; no completion line exists for any of the 7 killed cycles' helper invocations in the same file.

**Causal status**: confirmed

**Owning-path proof**:

- **Production entry point**: `~/.config/systemd/user/aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service` — `KillMode=control-group`, `TimeoutStartSec=1860` (verified via `systemctl --user cat aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service`). Traced to the installer, confirming this is the shipped default and not local drift: `KillMode=control-group` is hard-coded unconditionally in `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/schedulers-linux.sh:189` (`_install_scheduler_systemd`); `TimeoutStartSec` is computed in `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/schedulers-pulse.sh:566` as `_pulse_timeout_sec=$((PULSE_STALE_THRESHOLD_SECONDS + 60))`; `PULSE_STALE_THRESHOLD_SECONDS=1800` is itself a hard-coded default in `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/schedulers.sh:22` (1800 + 60 = 1860, matching the deployed unit exactly). No override was found in `~/.aidevops/config`, `~/.aidevops/state`, or `~/.aidevops/agents/custom` on this machine. (Related: GH#17442, the prior fix that added `TimeoutStartSec` in the first place so a hang wouldn't block all future timer activations.)
- **Call chain**: `pulse-dispatch-preflight-lib.sh:98-102` (`_cleanup_async_helper` = `cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh`, same pattern repeated at `:112-116` for `cleanup-stashes-async-helper.sh` and `:126-130` for `cleanup-remote-branches-async-helper.sh`) → `nohup "$helper" ... & disown $! 2>/dev/null || true` → forked child inherits the invoking shell's cgroup (cgroups are assigned at fork/exec time by the kernel; `nohup`/`disown` only affect `SIGHUP` delivery and shell job-control tracking, neither creates or moves the process to a new cgroup) → helper remains inside `aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service`'s cgroup → `KillMode=control-group` SIGKILLs every process in that cgroup when `TimeoutStartSec` expires, the helper included.
- **Integrated verification**: live `systemctl --user status` output (above) shows the helper's PIDs nested directly under the service's own `CGroup:` listing while the service is still within its timeout window; `journalctl` shows the helper's process class (`bash`) among the processes SIGKILLed during a `control-group` kill; the helper's own log (`cleanup_worktrees.log`) shows completions only for invocations that raced ahead of the parent's timeout, with no completion recorded for cycles that were killed.

**Causal code**:

```bash
# pulse-dispatch-preflight-lib.sh:92-106
# GH#20554: Worktree cleanup is moved to an async background job so a slow
# cleanup (20+ worktrees × 2-5s gh API calls each) never hits a hard timeout
# and blocks the pulse cycle. ...
local _cleanup_async_helper="${SCRIPT_DIR}/cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh"
if [[ -x "$_cleanup_async_helper" ]]; then
	nohup "$_cleanup_async_helper" \
		>>"${HOME}/.aidevops/logs/cleanup_worktrees.log" 2>&1 &
	disown $! 2>/dev/null || true
else
	run_stage_with_timeout "cleanup_worktrees" 60 cleanup_worktrees || true
fi
```

**Call-site sweep** (same vulnerable pattern, all three inside the one 30-line block):

```
pulse-dispatch-preflight-lib.sh:100-102  nohup cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh & disown       (GH#20554)
pulse-dispatch-preflight-lib.sh:114-116  nohup cleanup-stashes-async-helper.sh & disown          (GH#21997)
pulse-dispatch-preflight-lib.sh:128-130  nohup cleanup-remote-branches-async-helper.sh & disown  (GH#22415)
pulse-dispatch-preflight-lib.sh:63-65    nohup "$merge_routine" run & disown                     (pulse-merge kick — same pattern, not scoped by this issue)
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `aidevops setup --scope pulse` on a machine with a moderate-to-large worktree/PR backlog (enough that a full pulse cycle routinely runs past ~20-25 min).
2. Let the timer-driven `aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service` run for a few hours unattended.
3. During an active cycle, run `systemctl --user status aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service --no-pager -l` and confirm `cleanup-worktrees-async-helper.sh` (or the stash/remote-branch equivalents) appear nested under the service's own `CGroup:`.
4. Run `journalctl --user -u aidevops-supervisor-pulse.service --since "-4 hours"` and look for repeated `code=killed, status=9/KILL` / `Failed with result 'timeout'` entries.
5. Compare `~/.aidevops/logs/cleanup_worktrees.last-run` (epoch) against the timestamps of the killed cycles — completions only line up with cycles that happened to finish before the timeout.

## Workarounds Applied

- Ran `aidevops worktree registry prune -v` — removed 72 of 85 stale/dead-PID entries from `~/.aidevops/.agent-workspace/worktree-registry.db`.
- Ran `aidevops worktree clean --auto` then `aidevops worktree clean --auto --force-merged` manually, outside the stuck pulse cycle, to force a cleanup pass. Recovered only ~514 MB (1 of ~28 worktrees) since most remaining worktrees' branches are not yet detected as merged (open PRs, or dispatch-precreated worktrees whose branch was never opened as a PR) — the low-level cleanup logic itself is working correctly and conservatively; it is starved of the chance to run to completion by the parent cycle's kill loop.

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.32.216
- **Latest version**: 3.32.216
- **AI Assistant**: Claude Code
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21(1)-release
- **Working repo**: mesh-manager (worktree-fix-maintainer-gate-pin)
- **gh CLI**: gh version 2.89.0 (2026-03-26)

## Additional Context

- Related/prior fixes in the same lineage, for context: GH#17442 (added `TimeoutStartSec` so a hung cycle doesn't block *future* timer activations — that fix is working as designed; this issue is about what the timeout's own `KillMode=control-group` takes down with it), GH#20554 / GH#21997 / GH#22415 (added the three async helpers this issue concerns).
- Separately, and marked explicitly **unconfirmed**: why cycles routinely run long enough to hit the 31-minute timeout in the first place was not root-caused in this session. One candidate contributor observed live: `gh api` calls paginating closed/merged PR history per registered repo (e.g. `quality-feedback-helper.sh:905`, a bare `gh api ...pulls?state=closed&per_page=100... --paginate` in `--backfill` mode with no `_gh_with_timeout`-style wrapper, matching the exact anti-pattern already fixed once in GH#28323 for `pulse-merge-*.sh` but evidently not swept across the rest of the codebase). This is offered as a candidate worth auditing separately, not as a confirmed cause of the specific hangs in this report.

title: consolidated: isolate Pulse OpenCode runtime from interactive CLI
body:
_Supersedes #29220 — this issue is the consolidated spec._

## What

Create and operate a Pulse-owned OpenCode runtime so Pulse services and headless workers never depend on, repair, or mutate the user's interactive `opencode` installation. Setup, update, and maintenance paths must install and repair the pinned headless runtime at a framework-owned location such as `${HOME}/.aidevops/runtime/opencode-pulse/bin/opencode`; Pulse service definitions must pass that binary through `OPENCODE_BIN`; dispatch must validate and use only that runtime; and status output must distinguish the Pulse runtime from the interactive CLI.

## Why

Pulse diagnostics showed an available auto-dispatch queue while workers failed to launch. Per-worker logs contained `OpenCode version drift: installed=unknown, pin=1.18.9 -- reinstalling` followed by `Failed to restore OpenCode to 1.18.9 -- refusing headless launch`. Interactive and clean-environment checks could run OpenCode 1.18.9, demonstrating that PATH, nvm, or systemd-context differences can make the shared version guard falsely block dispatch.

The durable fix is runtime isolation rather than dispatch-time repair of a global or user installation. Pulse must remain fail-closed when its own runtime is genuinely invalid without allowing an unparseable version string alone to stop a working canary or trigger repeated API/comments activity.

## Reproducer

1. Run Pulse worker dispatch from its headless/systemd context while the interactive or clean-environment OpenCode CLI can execute version 1.18.9.
2. Leave auto-dispatch work available and inspect the corresponding per-worker Pulse log.
3. Observe `OpenCode version drift: installed=unknown, pin=1.18.9 -- reinstalling`, followed by `Failed to restore OpenCode to 1.18.9 -- refusing headless launch`, and no worker launch.
4. Confirm the same host can run OpenCode 1.18.9 interactively or in a clean environment, demonstrating that service-context runtime discovery—not a genuinely broken OpenCode binary—caused the stop.

**Expected:** Pulse resolves and validates its own pinned runtime independently of the user's CLI and launches the worker when that runtime's canary succeeds.

**Actual:** dispatch resolves or repairs the shared/user runtime, treats an `unknown` version probe as fatal, and refuses the headless launch even though OpenCode itself can run.

## How

### Files to Modify

Line references below were verified against the default-branch HEAD available during consolidation; re-run the complete-write-surface search before editing because this runtime is actively maintained.

- `.agents/scripts/shared-constants.sh:185-196` — scope `OPENCODE_PINNED_VERSION` to headless Pulse and add or rename the shared constant/helper for the Pulse-owned binary instead of resolving the user's `opencode` from PATH.
- `.agents/scripts/headless-runtime-helper.sh:49` and `.agents/scripts/headless-runtime-helper.sh:912` — derive `OPENCODE_BIN_DEFAULT` from the Pulse-owned runtime and keep the pre-launch guard on that binary.
- `.agents/scripts/headless-runtime-lib.sh:1491-1582`, `.agents/scripts/headless-runtime-lib.sh:1702-1722`, and `.agents/scripts/headless-runtime-lib.sh:1879-1883` — make version enforcement, binary validation, canary selection, and effective runtime propagation operate on the Pulse-owned binary; remove dispatch-time mutation of the interactive CLI.
- `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/tool-install.sh:2351-2353` and `.agents/scripts/setup/_services.sh:316-329` — install, verify, or repair the pinned Pulse runtime during setup, update, or maintenance rather than during worker dispatch.
- `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/schedulers-pulse.sh:235-272`, `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/schedulers-pulse.sh:380`, `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/schedulers-pulse.sh:470-472`, `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/schedulers-pulse.sh:569`, and `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/schedulers-pulse.sh:912` — resolve the Pulse-owned runtime and export `OPENCODE_BIN` in Linux systemd and macOS launchd service definitions.
- `.agents/scripts/pulse-wrapper-config.sh:368` — remove any remaining Pulse default that resolves the interactive `opencode` from PATH.
- `.agents/scripts/tool-version-check.sh:69-87` — report pinned Pulse runtime state separately from the interactive OpenCode CLI.
- `.agents/scripts/tests/test-tool-version-check-opencode.sh:79-238`, `.agents/scripts/tests/test-setup-opencode-cli.sh:5-347`, `.agents/scripts/tests/test-schedulers-pulse-interval.sh`, and `.agents/scripts/tests/test-headless-runtime-helper.sh:202-205,280-283` plus its sourced test modules — update existing pin, setup, scheduler, canary, and launch coverage and add the focused isolation regressions below.

Audit related call sites discovered at current HEAD before deciding whether they require edits: `.agents/scripts/headless-runtime-run.sh:103`, `.agents/scripts/headless-runtime-model.sh:528`, `.agents/scripts/headless-runtime-provider.sh:98-109`, `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/migrations.sh:409`, and `.agents/scripts/tests/test-resolve-pulse-runtime-binary.sh:181-431`.

### Complete Write Surface

Before editing, run:

```bash
git grep -n "OPENCODE_PINNED_VERSION\|OPENCODE_BIN\|opencode-pulse\|_enforce_opencode_version_pin" -- .agents/scripts
```

Use the results to audit every setup, scheduler, runtime, migration, status, and test call site. Do not change user shell startup files. Tests must not write to user-specific absolute paths; use sandboxed `$HOME` fixtures.

### Implementation Steps

1. Introduce a shared Pulse/headless runtime path, defaulting to a framework-owned location such as `$HOME/.aidevops/runtime/opencode-pulse/bin/opencode`.
2. Update setup/update/maintenance logic to install and verify `OPENCODE_PINNED_VERSION` at that path and preserve existing runtime-bundle activation and rollback behaviour.
3. Update Pulse service generation for systemd and launchd to export `OPENCODE_BIN` with the Pulse-owned binary.
4. Change `_enforce_opencode_version_pin` so it checks or repairs only the Pulse-owned binary. It must never reinstall, replace, or otherwise mutate the interactive user `opencode` found through PATH.
5. Make canary execution authoritative when version probing is inconclusive: if the version probe returns `unknown` but the Pulse-owned runtime canary succeeds, allow dispatch. If the Pulse-owned binary cannot run the canary, emit a clear `pulse_runtime_invalid` blocker (or equivalent) and stop dispatch without claim, API, or comment storms.
6. Keep interactive OpenCode status reporting separate from Pulse runtime status so diagnostics identify which installation is healthy or stale.

### Hazards and Compatibility

- Preserve fail-closed behaviour for a genuinely broken Pulse-owned runtime while removing false stops caused by user PATH, nvm, or systemd differences.
- Never change the user's interactive OpenCode installation during worker dispatch, version checks, or canary checks.
- Preserve existing rollback and runtime-bundle activation behaviour.
- Avoid creating a dispatch loop when GitHub authentication or rate limits already block issue metadata reads.

### Verification Before Dispatch

Run the existing focused suites:

```bash
bash .agents/scripts/tests/test-tool-version-check-opencode.sh
bash .agents/scripts/tests/test-setup-opencode-cli.sh
bash .agents/scripts/tests/test-schedulers-pulse-interval.sh
bash .agents/scripts/tests/test-headless-runtime-helper.sh
```

Add or update focused regression coverage proving that:

- a bad or missing interactive user `opencode` does not block Pulse when the Pulse-owned binary passes its canary;
- dispatch does not attempt to reinstall or mutate the interactive user CLI;
- an `unknown` version probe does not block a successful Pulse-owned canary;
- a broken Pulse-owned runtime emits the clear blocker and does not cause repeated claims, API calls, or comments.

Run ShellCheck with zero new violations for every edited shell script.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Pulse services use a Pulse-owned OpenCode binary through `OPENCODE_BIN`.
- [ ] Setup, update, and maintenance can install or repair the pinned Pulse runtime without altering the user's interactive OpenCode installation.
- [ ] Worker dispatch, version checks, and canary checks never mutate the interactive user `opencode`.
- [ ] A version probe returning `unknown` does not block dispatch when the Pulse-owned binary passes its canary.
- [ ] A broken Pulse-owned runtime produces a clear `pulse_runtime_invalid` blocker (or equivalent), fails closed, and does not create a worker claim/comment or API storm.
- [ ] Interactive and Pulse OpenCode status are reported separately.
- [ ] Existing rollback/runtime-bundle activation continues to work.
- [ ] The four listed shell test suites and focused isolation regressions pass using sandboxed `$HOME` fixtures.
- [ ] Edited shell scripts pass ShellCheck with zero regressions.

## Context & Decisions

- **Original problem statement:** the parent issue identified a false headless dispatch stop caused by sharing runtime discovery and repair with the interactive OpenCode installation.
- **Scope modifications from commenters:** none. No substantive comments were captured, so there are no commenter-added requirements to merge or attribute.
- **Final approach:** isolate Pulse behind a framework-owned pinned binary; provision it only through setup/update/maintenance; export it explicitly to Pulse services; validate only that runtime during dispatch; accept a successful canary when version text is `unknown`; fail closed with a clear, quiet blocker when that runtime cannot execute; and report interactive and Pulse installations independently.
- **Rejected or superseded approaches:** dispatch-time repair of the user's CLI, reliance on whichever `opencode` appears first in PATH, and treating an `unknown` version string by itself as proof that the runtime is unusable.
- **Attribution:** all substantive requirements and decisions above come from the original parent body. There were no substantive commenter contributions or unresolved comment-thread decisions.

## Contributors

cc: _No substantive comment authors detected._

title: consolidated: reduce tools.mjs file complexity without behavior changes
body:
_Supersedes #29212 — this issue is the consolidated spec._

## What

Remove the remaining `qlty:file-complexity` smell from `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tools.mjs` with the smallest behavior-preserving structural refactor. Preserve the exported plugin API, registered tool names and schemas, error text, security boundaries, timeout handling, and runtime behavior.

The original automated scan measured total complexity at 62 against a threshold of 49, a deficit of 13. Current default-branch validation still reproduces the same single smell: Qlty 0.636.0 reports `High total complexity (count = 51)` for the file. The target is therefore still unsatisfied even though recent refactoring reduced the count.

## Why

This is baseline maintainability repair, not evidence that an unrelated pull request introduced the smell. The file remains above the Qlty total-complexity limit, and low-density files remain eligible so distributed debt cannot evade remediation.

The repair must lower real structural complexity rather than move new smells into sibling files, inflate `QLTY_SMELL_THRESHOLD`, or use an unrelated-baseline override. Public behavior must not change.

## How

### Files to Modify

- `EDIT: .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tools.mjs:1-423` — retain the public `tool` binding at lines 6-34 and `createTools()` composition contract at lines 410-423 while reducing the file total-complexity score.
- `NEW: .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/pre-edit-tool.mjs` — extract the cohesive pre-edit implementation currently represented by `PRE_EDIT_GUIDANCE` at lines 169-173 and `formatPreEditCheckResult()`, `createPreEditCheckTool()`, and `runPreEditCheck()` at lines 284-380. Keep this sibling module internal and dependency-inject the existing `tool`/schema and worktree resolver as needed; do not create a second public entry point.
- `VERIFY: .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/test-pre-edit-tool-workdir.mjs:12-117` — preserve explicit-worktree validation, delayed loop-mode completion, and process-tree timeout coverage.
- `VERIFY: .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/test-tool-args-schema.mjs:11-44` — preserve all registered Zod-compatible schemas and triage isolation.
- `VERIFY: .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/test-memory-tool-schema.mjs:14-139` and `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/test-hook-status-tool.mjs:11-90` — prove the neighboring tool factories remain unchanged.

### Complete Write Surface

- **Callers/readers:** `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/index.mjs:54` imports `createTools`; `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/oauth-pool-tool.mjs:12` imports the public `tool` binding. Both imports must remain valid.
- **Writers/mutation paths:** only the module split and import/composition wiring above; no persistent-data writes or migrations exist.
- **Tests/fixtures:** the four focused test files listed above encode the affected schema, hook-status, memory, worktree, timeout, and process-group behavior.
- **Schemas/config:** `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/package.json:5-27` confirms ESM, the package test command, OpenCode compatibility metadata, and `@opencode-ai/plugin` dependency. No schema or dependency version change is required.
- **Generated/deployed mirrors:** source files under `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/` are canonical; do not edit deployed copies under the home directory.
- **Migrations/backfills:** none; this is a pure internal module refactor.
- **Cleanup/rollback:** reverting the extraction and import restores the original single-file layout; there is no state migration.

### Implementation Steps

1. Run the focused tests and Qlty command before editing to preserve baseline evidence.
2. Extract the pre-edit constants and functions into `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/pre-edit-tool.mjs`. Keep the existing return strings, default 120000 ms timeout, detached process-group termination, worktree validation, and error handling byte-for-byte equivalent where practical.
3. Import the internal factory into `tools.mjs` and keep `createTools(scriptsDir, run, options = {})`, the triage early return, `options.preEditTimeoutMs`, `options.workerWorktree`, the optional pool factory, and all public tool keys unchanged.
4. Re-run Qlty after the extraction. If the original file still has a smell, make the next-smallest cohesive extraction rather than adding indirection inside functions or transferring a smell to the new file. Do not alter behavior to satisfy the metric.
5. Run syntax, focused package tests, changed-file lint, and Qlty checks. No public API changes are permitted.

### Hazards and Compatibility

- `tools.mjs` uses top-level dynamic import fallback for `@opencode-ai/plugin`; preserve one shared `tool`/schema identity and avoid circular imports.
- `oauth-pool-tool.mjs` relies on the exported `tool` binding, while `index.mjs` and tests rely on `createTools`; both exports remain in `tools.mjs`.
- The pre-edit runner deliberately uses a detached child process and kills the complete process group on timeout. A split must not weaken that safety behavior or leave a helper running after timeout.
- Worktree resolution and hook inspection enforce repository boundaries and avoid exposing hook contents or paths. Do not broaden accepted targets or bypass symlink checks.
- This is dispatch-path code, so retain `tier:thinking`; model strength alone does not justify changing behavior or bypassing review/security gates.

Use only its general behavior-preservation, identity-key, and CI-justification principles. title: bug(pulse-merge-feedback): review-feedback routing truncates reviews to first line + marker lacks head-SHA (t2093)
body:
## Description

`_dispatch_pr_fix_worker()` in `.agents/scripts/pulse-merge-feedback.sh` is the deterministic-merge-pass path that routes a worker PR's `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review feedback into the linked issue body so a freshly dispatched worker can act on it (t2093). Two compounding defects in that path make the routed feedback useless and cause an infinite no-op loop:

1. **First-line-only truncation** (`_build_review_feedback_section`, lines 100 and 107): both the top-level-review and inline-comment jq filters do `((.body // "") | gsub("\r"; "") | split("\n")[0])[0:300]` — i.e. they keep only the text *before the first newline* of each review body (then cap at 300 chars). Any review whose body opens with a markdown heading followed by a blank line (the standard shape our senior-review template produces: `## Senior code review — REQUEST CHANGES\n\n<findings>`) gets reduced to just the heading. Every actual finding — BLOCK bugs, suggested fixes, file:line citations in the review body — is silently dropped.

2. **Idempotency marker has no head-SHA component** (`_dispatch_pr_fix_worker`, line 2003): `local marker="<!-- t2093:review-feedback:PR${pr_number} -->"` is keyed only by PR number. `_append_feedback_to_issue` (line 156) skips the append forever once this marker exists in the issue body, regardless of whether a later, materially different `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review lands on the same still-open PR after a push. The sibling conflict-feedback path has the identical gap: `local marker="<!-- conflict-feedback:PR${pr_number} -->"` (line 1894).

Notably, the *fix pattern for #2 already exists in this same file*: the CI-feedback-fallback path (added later, commit `c2fa0c266e`, 2026-07-13) uses `local marker_prefix="<!-- ci-feedback-fallback:PR${pr_number}:SHA${pr_head_sha:-unknown}"` (lines 565-566) — i.e. it re-routes whenever the PR head commit changes. The review-feedback (line 2003) and conflict-feedback (line 1894) markers were never updated to match, and both still date to the original t2093 commit `417fe81f39` (2026-04-19).

## Expected Behavior

- The routed "Review Feedback" section in the linked issue should contain the substantive body of each `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review (or a much larger truncation window / the full body), not just its first line.
- If a PR receives a *new* `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review after an earlier one was already routed (i.e. the PR's head SHA changed since the marker was written, or the review id/timestamp differs from what's already recorded), the merge pass should route the new review's content too — analogous to the SHA-qualified marker already used by the CI-feedback-fallback path.

## Reproducer

**Symptom command**:

```
~/.aidevops/agents/scripts/pulse-diagnose-helper.sh pr 3412 --repo Majowka/mesh-manager --verbose
gh issue view 3407 -R Majowka/mesh-manager --json body -q '.body'
```

**Actual output**:

pulse.log (646 events traced) shows the merge pass correctly deferring on `CHANGES_REQUESTED` every cycle (`pw-merge-skip-changes-requested`), then routing exactly once:

```
[pulse-wrapper] _dispatch_pr_fix_worker: routed review feedback from PR #3412 to issue #3407 in Majowka/mesh-manager (t2093)
```

The resulting section appended to issue #3407's body is:

```
<!-- t2093:review-feedback:PR3412 -->
## Review Feedback routed from PR #3412 (t2093)
...
### Top-level reviews

- **@kamcio2603** (`CHANGES_REQUESTED`): ## Senior code review — REQUEST CHANGES
  [view review](https://github.com/Majowka/mesh-manager/pull/3412#pullrequestreview-4827727592)
```

— i.e. the actual review content (a BLOCK finding: `App.tsx` references `RequireRole` without importing it, crashing the app for every user, plus a missing-test-coverage note) never made it into the issue. Worse, this routing captured a **different, earlier, already-superseded** review (submitted 2026-07-31T10:35:29Z, about failing CI, routed at 10:48:37) — the actual still-blocking review was submitted later that day (2026-07-31T11:46:04Z, at head commit `2567250d6889332d870ccd65c4886a1f10bcb795`, still HEAD as of this report) and was never routed, because the marker from the first routing already existed.

Three subsequent dispatches of issue #3407 (`DISPATCH_CLAIM`/`CLAIM_RELEASED reason=worker_complete` at 2026-07-31T09:32Z, 2026-07-31T11:18Z, and 2026-08-02T11:29Z, per issue-comment lifecycle log) each ended with a `post_pr_handoff` outcome in `headless-runtime-metrics.jsonl` — the worker found nothing actionable in the (content-free) routed feedback, saw the existing linked PR already appeared complete against the issue's acceptance criteria, and just reopened PR #3412 without pushing any commit. PR #3412's head stayed at `2567250d...` across all three cycles. Net effect: each cycle repeats the same four steps — close PR, route (no-op), redispatch, worker reopens the same PR unchanged, PR is still CHANGES_REQUESTED — with no forward progress across cycles.

**Expected output**:

The issue #3407 body should have contained the actual second review's findings (missing `RequireRole` import in `App.tsx:141`, missing test coverage for the new RBAC gating), giving the redispatched worker something concrete to fix instead of handing off.

**Causal status**: confirmed

**Owning-path proof**:

- **Production entry point**: `pulse-merge-feedback.sh:1953` `_dispatch_pr_fix_worker()`, invoked by the deterministic merge pass's `_check_pr_merge_gates` when a self-authored worker PR has `reviewDecision=CHANGES_REQUESTED` (see file header, lines 9-15).
- **Call chain**: `_dispatch_pr_fix_worker` (1953) calls `gh api repos/.../pulls/${pr_number}/reviews` (1974), then `_build_review_feedback_section` (1995, defined 70) where line 100/107 truncate each body to `split("\n")[0]`, then `_append_feedback_to_issue` (2004, defined 138) where line 156 gates on the PR-number-only marker built at line 2003, permanently skipping (line 160 log: `already has routed feedback marker for this PR — skipping`) once set.
- **Integrated verification**: live production trace via `pulse-diagnose-helper.sh pr 3412 --repo Majowka/mesh-manager` (pulse.log, 646 events) shows the single `pw-route-review-fix` firing matching this exact call path, and the live GitHub issue #3407 body contains the marker plus the truncated content exactly as the code at lines 100/156 would produce. `headless-runtime-metrics.jsonl` for issue #3407 shows 3× `post_pr_handoff` results, no code-change attempts, confirming the downstream worker-loop consequence.

**Causal code**:

```bash
git blame .agents/scripts/pulse-merge-feedback.sh -L 100,100
# 417fe81f39 (Marcus Quinn 2026-04-19 04:36:28 +0100 100) .[] | "- **@\(.author)** (`\(.state)`): \(((.body // "") | gsub("\r"; "") | split("\n")[0])[0:300])\n  [view review](\(.url // ""))"

git blame .agents/scripts/pulse-merge-feedback.sh -L 2003,2003
# 417fe81f39 (Marcus Quinn 2026-04-19 04:36:28 +0100 2003) local marker="<!-- t2093:review-feedback:PR${pr_number} -->"

# Sibling fix pattern already proven in the same file for the CI-feedback path:
git blame .agents/scripts/pulse-merge-feedback.sh -L 565,566
# c2fa0c266e (Marcus Quinn 2026-07-13 17:25:24 +0100 565) local marker_prefix="<!-- ci-feedback-fallback:PR${pr_number}:SHA${pr_head_sha:-unknown}"
# c2fa0c266e (Marcus Quinn 2026-07-13 17:25:24 +0100 566) local marker="${marker_prefix} -->"
```

**Call-site sweep**:

```bash
grep -n 'split("\\n")\[0\]\|local marker=\"<!-- ' .agents/scripts/pulse-merge-feedback.sh
# 100:  ...split("\n")[0])[0:300])...       <- truncation bug, review-feedback path
# 107:  ...split("\n")[0])[0:300])...       <- truncation bug, review-feedback path (inline comments)
# 1894: local marker="<!-- conflict-feedback:PR${pr_number} -->"      <- same PR-only marker gap (conflict-routing sibling; not independently reproduced live in this report, flagged by pattern match only)
# 2003: local marker="<!-- t2093:review-feedback:PR${pr_number} -->" <- confirmed marker gap, this report's live symptom
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a worker-authored PR receive a `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review whose body opens with a heading line (e.g. `## Senior code review — REQUEST CHANGES`) followed by the actual findings on later lines.
2. Let the deterministic merge pass route it once (`_dispatch_pr_fix_worker` fires, PR closes, issue gets `<!-- t2093:review-feedback:PR<N> -->` + a first-line-only stub).
3. Push a new commit to the reopened/redispatched PR and have a human leave a *second*, more specific `CHANGES_REQUESTED` review.
4. Observe: the merge pass logs `already has routed feedback marker for this PR — skipping` and never appends the second review's content; redispatched workers see no actionable feedback and emit `POST_PR_HANDOFF` on every subsequent dispatch.

## Workarounds Applied

None. This was a diagnostic-only session (`pulse-diagnose-helper.sh pr/issue`, manual `gh` inspection, `git blame`) — no manual edit was made to PR #3412, issue #3407, or the framework scripts. The underlying RBAC bug in mesh-manager PR #3412 (missing `RequireRole` import in `App.tsx`) is still unfixed and is being handled separately in that repo.

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.32.216
- **Latest version**: 3.32.216
- **Install method**: unknown (/home/ubuntu/.local/bin/aidevops)
- **AI Assistant**: Claude Code (Sonnet 5)
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21(1)-release
- **Working repo**: Majowka/mesh-manager, worktree `fix-maintainer-gate-pin` (observing repo; the bug is in the aidevops framework itself)
- **gh CLI**: gh version 2.89.0 (2026-03-26)

## Additional Context

Observed on `Majowka/mesh-manager` PR #3412 / issue #3407, but the defective code is generic to any repo running the aidevops pulse deterministic merge pass — this is a framework bug, not a mesh-manager-specific one. Suggested minimal fix: (a) widen or remove the `split("\n")[0]` first-line truncation at lines 100/107 so routed reviews carry their actual findings; (b) extend the `marker`/`marker_prefix` at lines 1894 and 2003 to include the PR head SHA, mirroring the already-shipped pattern at lines 565-566, so a new review after a new push gets routed instead of silently suppressed.

title: consolidated: reduce provider auth request file complexity
body:
_Supersedes #29211 — this issue is the consolidated spec._

<!-- aidevops:brief-schema=v2 -->
<!-- aidevops:generator=function-complexity-sweep cited_file=.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs smell_count=1 actual=62 threshold=49 deficit=13 -->

## What

Refactor `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs` so Qlty no longer reports its single `qlty:file-complexity` smell. The result must be a purely structural, behavior-preserving simplification: request headers, request-body transformations, URL rewriting, response-stream handling, exported symbols, and callers must behave exactly as before.

## Why

The automated quality sweep measured file complexity at **62** against a threshold of **49**, a deficit of **13**. This is verified default-branch baseline debt, not evidence that an unrelated pull request introduced a regression. Repairing low-density files is intentional so distributed complexity debt cannot evade the repository threshold.

The target has not changed since commit `53d0d67bd504675a843c20d537aeca126634913f` (2026-05-05), which predates the 2026-08-02 scan. No open or closed PR referencing #29211, no issue branch, and no existing consolidated successor were found during consolidation.

## How

### Files and current boundaries

- `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs:32-90` — request-header helpers and the exported `buildRequestHeaders()` API.
- `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs:97-378` — system-prompt, tool-schema, tool-name, and request-body transformations, including exported `injectIntentParameter()` and `transformRequestBody()`.
- `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs:384-405` — URL parsing and exported `addBetaQueryParam()`.
- `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs:411-475` — response-stream prefix reversal, chunk buffering, and exported `transformResponseStream()`.
- `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth.mjs:34,284-302` — existing consumer contract; preserve these imported names and behavior.
- `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/test-intent-schema-injection.mjs:33-240` and `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/test-provider-auth-cch.mjs:13-54` — focused regression coverage for two exported request transformations.

### Implementation approach

1. Record the Qlty baseline, then apply the smallest coherent refactor that removes the file-level smell. Measure after each change and stop once the target is below the threshold.
2. Prefer a cohesive ESM extraction over cosmetic churn. The first bounded candidate is the response-stream block at `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs:407-475`, extracted to a sibling such as `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-stream.mjs`. Keep `transformResponseStream` available from the original module through an ESM re-export so existing consumers do not change.
3. If that extraction alone does not clear the measured deficit, extract the body-transform cluster at `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs:97-378` to a cohesive sibling such as `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-body.mjs`, again preserving the original module's exports. Do not split individual branches merely to game the score.
4. Preserve all constants, key ordering, billing-header hash behavior, tool-name mappings, `agent__intent` schema semantics, system-message redistribution, SSE line buffering, and `Response` metadata exactly.
5. Add or adjust focused tests for any moved boundary. If response streaming moves, cover an MCP tool name split across stream chunks so the buffering invariant at current lines 423-461 remains protected.
6. The parent cited `.agents/reference/large-file-split.md` plus the simple `issue-sync-helper.sh`/`issue-sync-lib.sh` and complex `headless-runtime-lib.sh`/sub-library precedents. Its current scope at lines 56-66 explicitly excludes non-shell splits, so do **not** copy their shell include guards or `SCRIPT_DIR` mechanics into these ESM modules. Use only their general orchestration, identity-key, and justified-gate guidance, and follow the existing sibling ESM pattern in `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/`.
7. If a legitimate split creates a known identity-key or new-file gate artifact, apply the parent-specified `ratchet-bump` label and include a `## Complexity Bump Justification` section in the PR body with the before/after measurement and Qlty smell reduction. Use a gate-specific override only for a demonstrated artifact, never for a new PR-specific smell.

### Verification

Run the repository's current Node checks and focused tests:

```bash
node --check .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs
node --test \
  .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/test-intent-schema-injection.mjs \
  .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/test-provider-auth-cch.mjs
node --test .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/tests/*.mjs
qlty smells .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs --no-snippets --quiet
```

Also run `node --check` and `qlty smells --no-snippets --quiet` against each new `.mjs` file. During consolidation, Node v26.4.0 syntax checking and the two focused suites passed (14 tests); the local runner did not have the Qlty CLI installed, so the implementation worker must obtain the terminal smell result from its environment or CI.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `qlty smells .agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/provider-auth-request.mjs --no-snippets --quiet` no longer reports `qlty:file-complexity` for the target.
- [ ] Any new module is cohesive, below applicable smell thresholds, and introduces no new PR-specific Qlty findings.
- [ ] Existing exports remain available from `provider-auth-request.mjs`; `provider-auth.mjs` callers require no public API migration.
- [ ] Header construction, billing/hash serialization, system-prompt redistribution, tool-schema injection, tool-name normalization, URL rewriting, and response-stream output remain behaviorally identical.
- [ ] SSE tool names split across chunks remain buffered and normalized correctly.
- [ ] Focused tests, the complete OpenCode plugin Node test suite, and syntax checks pass.
- [ ] `QLTY_SMELL_THRESHOLD` and unrelated-baseline overrides are unchanged.
- [ ] Any gate override is limited to a measured split identity artifact and is documented in a `## Complexity Bump Justification` PR section.

## Context & Decisions

- The automated quality-sweep author supplied the original problem, metrics, constraints, reference pattern, verification commands, and dispatch policy in #29211.
- No substantive comments were captured, so no commenter added, rejected, corrected, or superseded any part of the scope.
- The final approach remains the original one: the smallest behavior-preserving structural refactor that removes the verified smell, with no API or behavior changes.
- The current large-file-split reference is shell-specific; its shell mechanics are not applicable to this JavaScript target. Existing ESM sibling-module conventions are the applicable implementation pattern.
- `needs-maintainer-review` is not carried forward: the source policy reserves that gate for an actual behavior, API, security, or architecture trade-off, and none is part of this bounded cleanup. The successor is explicitly handed to autonomous dispatch at `tier:thinking`.
- New PR-specific smells remain blocking. Neither threshold inflation nor an unrelated-baseline override may absorb findings introduced by this repair.

title: bug(linux): recoverable worktree archives bypass the system Trash
body:
## Description

Recoverable worktree removal now copies each worktree and its Git administrative state into a unique bucket under `$HOME/.Trash` before removing the source. The archive-first safety model introduced by #28822 is valuable, but the default destination assumes macOS Trash semantics on every platform.

On Linux, `$HOME/.Trash` is not the Freedesktop Trash. GNOME/GIO and other conforming tools use `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/Trash` (with mount-specific Trash locations where applicable). As a result, aidevops recovery buckets on Linux are ordinary hidden directories: they are not listed by system Trash tools, are not removed by “Empty Trash”, and can consume substantial disk space without the operator seeing them in the desktop Trash.

A read-only audit on one high-activity Ubuntu installation found:

- 60 current `aidevops-worktree-cleanup-*` recovery buckets under `$HOME/.Trash`, allocated at 8,379,465,728 bytes;
- 288 older worktree entries in the Freedesktop Trash, allocated at 32,077,869,056 bytes;
- zero `$HOME/.Trash` entries visible through `gio trash --list`.

This report does not prescribe moving the coupled recovery bucket directly into Freedesktop Trash. Maintainers should decide whether these artifacts are intended to be normal OS Trash entries or durable aidevops recovery data. The current Linux behavior is problematic under either interpretation: the path is named and implemented as Trash, but Linux does not treat it as Trash and no separate recovery-store contract is presented to the operator.

## Expected Behavior

Recoverable worktree storage should have explicit, platform-correct semantics:

- If it is OS Trash, use the platform Trash API/location so Linux tools can list, restore, and empty it correctly.
- If it must survive normal “Empty Trash”, use a clearly named aidevops-owned recovery location with an explicit inventory and lifecycle contract.

The archive-before-remove guarantees from #28822 must remain intact. A platform fix must not weaken lock, identity, late-write, staged-state, detached-HEAD, or interruption recovery.

## Reproducer

**Symptom command**:

```bash
gio trash --list | python3 -c 'import sys; x=sys.stdin.read(); print({"listed_entries":len(x.splitlines()),"home_dot_trash_entries":x.count("/.Trash/")})'

fd --hidden --max-depth 1 --type d '^aidevops-worktree-cleanup-' "$HOME/.Trash" | wc -l

du -sB1 -- "$HOME/.local/share/Trash" "$HOME/.Trash"
```

**Actual output**:

```text
{'listed_entries': 288, 'home_dot_trash_entries': 0}
60
32077869056  $HOME/.local/share/Trash
8379465728   $HOME/.Trash
```

**Blocked command**: Not applicable. The archive operation completed; this is a completed-path platform semantics defect, not a hang or timeout.

**Backend state**: Not applicable. No API budget, rate limit, transport, or remote-service cause is asserted.

The recovery buckets were created during normal aidevops worktree cleanup. No archive was moved, restored, or deleted during diagnosis.

**Expected output**:

The Linux operator should be able to identify the destination as either system Trash or an aidevops recovery store, and the relevant platform/operator tooling should report it consistently. A directory named `$HOME/.Trash` should not silently stand in for system Trash on Linux.

**Causal status**: confirmed

**Owning-path proof**:

- **Production entry point**: `.agents/scripts/worktree-helper-cmds.sh:400-417` archives manual removals before native Git removal; `.agents/scripts/worktree-clean-lib.sh:1274-1294,1345-1369` does the same for recoverable automated cleanup; `.agents/scripts/profile-readme-helper.sh:141-153` uses the shared archive helper for publication worktrees.
- **Call chain**: removal caller → `archive_worktree_path_recoverably()` → default `trash_root="${HOME}/.Trash"` at `.agents/scripts/audit-worktree-removal-helper.sh:694-735` → copied worktree/admin state and recovery sidecar → `remove_archived_worktree_path()` at `:950-989` → native Git source removal.
- **Integrated verification**: 59 of 60 current buckets had readable archived HEAD/index state and clean Git status; one interrupted/incomplete bucket remained recoverable for manual review. GIO listed none of those buckets, confirming the production archive path and the Linux Trash visibility mismatch end to end.

**Causal code/history**:

```text
24e30954fb19 / #28822 / PR #28832 introduced archive-before-remove recovery.
.agents/scripts/audit-worktree-removal-helper.sh:717-720 selects $HOME/.Trash when no override is set.
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run aidevops on Linux with no `AIDEVOPS_WORKTREE_TRASH_ROOT` or `AIDEVOPS_ORPHAN_TRASH_ROOT` override.
2. Let a guarded worktree removal complete through the archive-first path.
3. Observe an `aidevops-worktree-cleanup-*` bucket under `$HOME/.Trash`.
4. Run `gio trash --list` or inspect the desktop Trash.
5. Observe that the bucket is absent and remains after normal “Empty Trash”.

## Workarounds Applied

- Performed a read-only safety audit of both Linux Trash locations.
- Froze a point-in-time manifest and classified archives using Git state, remote/merge evidence, task state, unique-file checks, and live-process references.
- Did not use “Empty Trash”, because it would affect the Freedesktop entries but leave `$HOME/.Trash` untouched.
- Did not delete, move, restore, compress, prune, reset, or garbage-collect anything.

## Files and Existing Patterns to Examine

- `.agents/scripts/audit-worktree-removal-helper.sh:694-753,950-989` — archive destination, coupled recovery layout, and archive-bound removal.
- `.agents/scripts/worktree-helper-cmds.sh:370-427` — manual removal archive path.
- `.agents/scripts/worktree-clean-lib.sh:1274-1375` — automated recoverable cleanup path.
- `.agents/scripts/profile-readme-helper.sh:141-175` — profile publication cleanup.
- `.agents/scripts/pulse-todo-sync-workspace.sh:307-329` and `.agents/scripts/pulse-cleanup.sh:495-528` — other Linux-relevant `$HOME/.Trash` fallback semantics that may need a consistent platform decision.
- `.agents/reference/storage-lifecycle.md:59-70,128-183` — ownership, OS Trash, reporting, and producer-specific lifecycle contract.
- `.agents/scripts/tests/test-worktree-removal-audit.sh` — archive integrity and interruption fixtures; add Linux/macOS destination semantics without destructive live-home testing.

## Considerations for Maintainers

1. **Do not collapse safety into path selection.** The recovery bucket includes copied Git admin/index state and identity binding; a generic file move may not preserve that contract without adaptation.
2. **Clarify ownership.** Normal OS Trash is external/joint and user-controlled. A durable recovery store is framework-owned and needs reporting, protection reasons, and cleanup authority.
3. **Cover Linux generally.** Ubuntu/GNOME is the observed reproducer, but the mismatch concerns Linux/Freedesktop Trash semantics, including desktop and headless hosts.
4. **Preserve macOS behavior intentionally.** `$HOME/.Trash` is meaningful on macOS; tests should validate the chosen policy rather than hardcoding one path across platforms.
5. **Handle existing buckets.** A fix for new archives should report or conservatively migrate attributable legacy `$HOME/.Trash/aidevops-worktree-cleanup-*` buckets instead of abandoning them.
6. **Keep deletion separate.** Correcting the path must not authorize broad Empty Trash or deletion of dirty, unique, unpushed, active, or unknown recovery data.

## Suggested Validation Outcomes

- Linux and macOS fixtures select and report the intended storage semantics without touching a live user Trash.
- Archive integrity, lock races, late writes, staged/untracked state, detached HEAD, and interruption recovery from #28822 remain covered.
- Linux system Trash tooling either sees the archive by design, or aidevops clearly reports a separate recovery store by design.
- Existing attributable buckets have a fail-closed inventory/migration path.
- Focused shell tests, ShellCheck, and changed-file lint pass.

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.32.216
- **Latest version**: 3.32.216
- **AI Assistant**: OpenCode
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21
- **gh CLI**: 2.96.0

## Duplicate and Recent-Change Checks

- #28822 / PR #28832 intentionally introduced the current archive-first safety design but did not address Linux Trash semantics.
- #22417 / PR #22426 reduced system Trash growth for verified permanent-removal paths; later archive-first changes reintroduced a recovery copy for the affected paths.
- #28123 established the broader storage-lifecycle architecture, but recoverable worktree buckets are not currently presented as a producer-owned store.
- Searches for Linux/Freedesktop worktree Trash paths and `AIDEVOPS_WORKTREE_TRASH_ROOT` found no open issue covering this mismatch.

## Tier Rationale

`tier:thinking`: maintainers must reconcile a confirmed cross-platform path bug with a deliberate destructive-safety and recovery boundary. The issue asks for an explicit platform/ownership decision, not a blind path substitution.

title: bug(setup): skip macOS-only Automator MCP install and updates on non-macOS hosts
body:
## Description

Aidevops installs and refreshes the macOS Automator MCP as though it were cross-platform. On the observed Ubuntu host, `macos-automator-mcp` is installed under the global npm prefix even though the package provides AppleScript/JXA automation and is explicitly marked macOS-only elsewhere in the framework.

Two production paths lack the operating-system guard already used by runtime configuration generation:

- `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/mcp-setup.sh:21-45` includes `@steipete/macos-automator-mcp` in the unconditional global Node MCP installation loop.
- `.agents/scripts/tool-version-check.sh:120-133` includes it in the unconditional npm freshness list, with an update command that installs `@latest`.

By contrast, `.agents/scripts/generate-runtime-config-mcp.sh:80-85` correctly checks for Darwin, and `.agents/plugins/opencode-aidevops/mcp-registry.mjs:140-147` records `macOnly: true`.

## Expected Behavior

On Linux and other non-macOS systems, aidevops should not install or update the macOS Automator MCP. Existing platform-aware registration behaviour should remain unchanged on macOS.

## Reproducer

**Symptom command**:

```bash
command -v macos-automator-mcp
```

**Actual output**:

```text
~/.npm-global/bin/macos-automator-mcp
```

The host is Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS. Source inspection confirms that the setup installer and freshness updater include the package without an OS condition.

**Expected output**:

No binary should be installed by aidevops on a non-macOS host, and routine freshness checks should skip the package.

**Causal status**: confirmed

**Owning-path proof**:

- **Production entry point**: aidevops setup invokes `_install_mcp_packages_node()` in `.agents/scripts/setup/modules/mcp-setup.sh`; idle tool maintenance invokes `.agents/scripts/auto-update-freshness-lib.sh:622-626`.
- **Call chain**: `_install_mcp_packages_node()` iterates the unconditional `node_mcps` list and calls `npm_global_install "${pkg}@latest"`; the freshness path iterates the unconditional `NPM_TOOLS` list and executes its update command when outdated.
- **Integrated verification**: the macOS-only binary is present in the Ubuntu global npm prefix, while the cited production lists contain the package without platform filtering.

**Causal code**:

```text
3bcbbe38b8 — added the macOS Automator MCP to the generic npm tool list
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run aidevops MCP setup on Ubuntu or another non-macOS host.
2. Inspect the global package commands.
3. Observe `macos-automator-mcp` is installed despite the host not supporting its Apple automation features.
4. Run or inspect the routine tool freshness path and observe the same package is eligible for updates.

## Workarounds Applied

None. The package was not removed because this session was limited to investigation and issue filing.

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.32.216
- **AI assistant**: OpenCode
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21
- **gh CLI**: 2.96.0

## Additional Context

Please review all installation, update, migration, and registration call sites for this package rather than correcting only one list. Existing Darwin checks in `.agents/scripts/generate-runtime-config-mcp.sh:80-85` and the `macOnly` registry field provide reference patterns. Preserve normal installation and update behaviour on macOS.

Suggested focused verification: Linux fixtures must omit the package from setup and update actions; Darwin fixtures must retain it; migration or cleanup behaviour for an already-installed copy should be conservative and explicitly decided rather than assumed. Duplicate searches for `macos-automator-mcp`, Linux, and tool updates found no matching open issue.

title: bug(tool updates): pinned OpenCode is reinstalled when registry latest is newer
body:
## Description

When OpenCode is deliberately pinned, the routine tool freshness path still compares the installed version with the registry's newest version. If the registry version is newer, the tool is classified as outdated, but the generated update command reinstalls the configured pin. This can repeatedly reinstall the same already-correct OpenCode version.

On the observed host, `OPENCODE_PINNED_VERSION` and the installed version are both `1.18.9`. Existing auto-update traces nevertheless contain repeated commands ending in `npm install -g opencode-ai@1.18.9` while a newer registry release exists.

This report is scoped to the clear comparison/update mismatch. It does not propose removing the safety pin. Ref #29296 covers the larger separation of interactive and Pulse-owned OpenCode runtimes; maintainers can decide whether this leaf fix should land independently or within that work.

## Expected Behavior

When the installed OpenCode version matches the version aidevops currently approves, routine freshness checks should not reinstall it. A newer upstream release may be reported for awareness, but should not make an already-correct pinned installation actionable.

## Reproducer

**Symptom command**:

```bash
.agents/scripts/tool-version-check.sh --update --quiet
```

This command was invoked by the idle-gated production path in `.agents/scripts/auto-update-freshness-lib.sh:622-626`; it was not rerun during this investigation because doing so would mutate the npm cache and global installation.

**Actual output**:

Relevant existing production trace, observed at least twice in `~/.aidevops/logs/auto-update.log`:

```text
Running: ... npm install -g opencode-ai@1.18.9
```

Current state:

```text
OPENCODE_PINNED_VERSION=1.18.9
opencode --version=1.18.9
```

**Expected output**:

OpenCode should be treated as up to date because the installed version matches the approved pin; no install command should run.

**Causal status**: confirmed

**Owning-path proof**:

- **Production entry point**: `.agents/scripts/auto-update-freshness-lib.sh:622-626` executes `tool-version-check.sh --update --quiet` during idle-gated tool freshness checks.
- **Call chain**: `.agents/scripts/tool-version-check.sh:87` builds an update command using `OPENCODE_PINNED_VERSION`; line 121 registers `opencode-ai` as an ordinary npm tool; lines 423-435 query registry latest; lines 476-481 mark an older installed version actionable; lines 689-729 execute the update command, which reinstalls the pin rather than registry latest.
- **Integrated verification**: the production auto-update log contains the generated pinned install command at least twice while the installed version already reports `1.18.9`.

**Causal code**:

```text
05495d6fd9 — GH#28892: Advance OpenCode headless pin safely
```

That commit correctly advanced the pin and centralized the repair command, while the generic npm latest-version comparison remained active.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure `OPENCODE_PINNED_VERSION` to a version older than registry latest.
2. Install that exact pinned version.
3. Run the tool freshness updater.
4. Observe that OpenCode is classified as outdated and the same pinned version is reinstalled.

## Workarounds Applied

None. The cache investigation was read-only after an earlier accidental npm cache verification; the tool update command was not rerun.

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.32.216
- **AI assistant**: OpenCode
- **OpenCode version**: 1.18.9
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21
- **gh CLI**: 2.96.0

## Additional Context

Likely implementation surfaces are `.agents/scripts/tool-version-check.sh`, `.agents/scripts/shared-constants.sh`, and `.agents/scripts/tests/test-tool-version-check-opencode.sh`. Please preserve the pin and fail-closed headless protections. Focused tests should prove that matching the pin causes no update, while genuine drift from the pin remains repairable and an upstream release can still be reported without triggering installation.

Duplicate discovery found #29296, which includes broader runtime isolation and separate status reporting, but not this narrowly reproduced pinned-version comparison bug. Closed #29002 addressed OpenCode self-updating past the pin rather than routine freshness reinstalling the already-installed pin.

title: Enhancement: add lifecycle visibility and guided cleanup for recoverable worktree archives
body:
## Description

Please evaluate a focused lifecycle and operator-safety contract for recoverable worktree archives created by aidevops.

The archive-before-remove design from #28822 protects against lock races, late writes, interruptions, staged state, and detached HEAD loss. However, each successful removal leaves a complete recovery bucket, and the current release provides no archive-specific count/byte visibility, warning threshold, safe-candidate report, guided cleanup, or producer-owned expiry path.

This is intentionally a design/enhancement request rather than a prescribed implementation. Maintainers should decide how worktree recovery fits the existing storage-lifecycle architecture, what evidence makes an archive reclaimable, and which existing status/maintenance surfaces should own warnings and cleanup guidance.

The Linux path mismatch is filed separately as #29309. Correcting that path alone will not solve lifecycle growth: on macOS, `$HOME/.Trash` is visible to Finder, but recovery worktrees still accumulate until the user manually empties Trash; on Linux, the current location is additionally invisible to system Trash tools.

## Observed Context

A read-only point-in-time audit on one high-activity installation found:

| Result | Count | Estimated allocated space |
|---|---:|---:|
| Safe candidate after state/evidence checks | 327 | 37,906,059,264 bytes |
| Must retain | 6 | about 1.32 GB |
| Insufficient evidence | 15 | about 1.23 GB |
| Verified duplicate | 0 | 0 bytes |
| **Total** | **348** | **40,457,334,784 bytes** |

The audit did not classify by age alone. It checked, where possible:

- archived repository, branch, and HEAD identity;
- whether the commit still existed locally and was pushed/merged;
- tracked changes, untracked files, and ignored files that might be unique;
- open/completed task evidence;
- active process, session, and registered-worktree references;
- duplicate recoverability.

Important exceptions demonstrated why broad Empty Trash or age-only deletion is unsafe:

- one archive contained 1,865 uncommitted tracked changes;
- several contained unique ignored task/recovery data;
- some linked tasks remained open;
- one recovery bucket was incomplete and differed from a later copy;
- small unique runtime-state files prevented strict “no unique files” proof.

At the same time, manually reconstructing this evidence across hundreds of archives was expensive. The archive producer already records much of the required identity at creation time, suggesting a producer-owned report could avoid repeated full filesystem scans.

## Expected Behavior

Operators should be able to understand and safely act on recoverable worktree storage without manually reverse-engineering Git metadata or choosing between “never clean” and “Empty Trash”.

Desired outcomes:

- Archive count and allocated bytes are visible before disk pressure becomes serious.
- Reporting distinguishes protected, reclaimable, and unknown archives with reasons.
- Dirty, unique, unpushed, active, or ambiguous work is never treated as reclaimable.
- Clean, pushed/merged/completed archives can be presented as candidates after revalidation.
- Cleanup is targeted, previewable, concurrency-aware, and explicit about the no-rollback boundary.
- Growth converges under an accepted policy without weakening #28822 recovery guarantees.

## Relationship to Existing Architecture

#28123 established `.agents/reference/storage-lifecycle.md` and a producer-owned, fail-closed model: ownership classes, protected/recovery/archive/cache states, soft candidate limits, hard safety vetoes, read-only reporting, and store-specific cleanup authority.

Recoverable worktree archives appear to be a focused missing producer contract:

- `.agents/reference/storage-lifecycle.md:49-57` says recovery data is retained until terminal state and recovery verification, while archive data receives a documented lifecycle.
- `:128-145` requires framework-owned stores to publish total/protected/reclaimable/unknown bytes, protection evidence, limits, next evaluation, and a store-specific dry-run/cleanup command.
- `:169-183` calls for a read-only operator surface and defers generic aggregate deletion in favour of producer-specific contracts.
- The initial inventory at `:59-70` mentions OS Trash generically but does not identify archive-before-remove worktree buckets as a producer with a convergence policy.

#22417 / PR #22426 previously reduced system Trash growth by permanently removing verified cleanup paths. #28822 / PR #28832 later added archive-before-remove recovery to close stronger lock/race/interruption hazards. The current enhancement should reconcile those valid goals rather than reverting either safety model wholesale.

## Considerations for Maintainers

Please explore the appropriate product and architecture boundary rather than treating these as fixed implementation requirements:

1. **Operator visibility** — Decide whether archive count, bytes, growth rate, free-space impact, and oldest candidate belong in `aidevops status`, storage inventory, session greeting advisories, Pulse diagnostics, or another existing surface.
2. **Warning policy** — Consider count, bytes, percentage of free disk, growth rate, or combined soft thresholds. Warnings should be actionable and rate-limited rather than repeated every session.
3. **State-based candidates** — Age may select candidates but must never prove safety. Revalidate clean state, unique files, local/remote commits, merged/completed status, ownership/claims, live processes/sessions, and exact archive identity.
4. **Creation-time evidence** — Extend the existing recovery sidecar/receipt if needed so later inventory does not rescan millions of dependency/cache files merely to rediscover known archive state. Mutable facts still require current revalidation.
5. **Protected exceptions** — Dirty or unique work, unpushed commits, active tasks, unreadable metadata, incomplete buckets, symlinks, identity changes, and failed reference checks remain protected/unknown.
6. **Guided cleanup** — Consider a read-only audit/plan followed by explicit application to exact manifest entries. Do not use broad Empty Trash or a generic recursive cleaner.
7. **Concurrency** — Snapshot candidates, acquire appropriate producer locks/leases, and recheck mutable evidence immediately before each deletion so parallel aidevops sessions remain safe.
8. **Rollback boundary** — Explain that the archive is itself the rollback copy. Permanent deletion has no rollback without independent backup; interruption should leave a clear original/staged state.
9. **Platform behavior** — Coordinate with #29309. macOS system Trash, Linux Freedesktop Trash, headless Linux, and mount-specific Trash have different operator semantics even if the safety classification policy is shared.
10. **Existing archives** — New limits alone leave current attributable buckets behind. Provide a conservative migration/inventory path for legacy standard-Trash entries and current recovery buckets.
11. **Generated content** — Dependency trees and caches may be reproducible, but ignored paths can also contain unique task data. Avoid blanket assumptions based only on ignore status.
12. **Default policy** — The audit is one high-activity installation. Validate warning and retention defaults across routine installations before enabling automatic expiry.

## Potential Operator Flow for Evaluation

This is an example for discussion, not a required command design:

1. Read-only inventory reports total, protected, reclaimable, and unknown archives.
2. A plan records exact archive identity, evidence, expected bytes, and exclusions.
3. The user reviews the plan and accepts the permanent-deletion boundary.
4. Apply operates in small batches, revalidating each archive and stopping on any mismatch.
5. Post-check confirms protected archives remain, expected paths disappeared, and actual free space increased.

## Files and Patterns to Examine

- `.agents/scripts/audit-worktree-removal-helper.sh:605-753,950-989` — recovery sidecar, archive identity, destination, and archive-bound removal.
- `.agents/scripts/worktree-helper-cmds.sh:370-427` — manual archive producer.
- `.agents/scripts/worktree-clean-lib.sh:1274-1375` — automated recoverable archive producer.
- `.agents/scripts/profile-readme-helper.sh:141-175` — periodic publication archives.
- `.agents/scripts/storage-inventory-helper.sh` — existing read-only ownership/safety reporting surface.
- `.agents/reference/storage-lifecycle.md` — accepted lifecycle and convergence architecture.
- `.agents/scripts/tests/test-worktree-removal-audit.sh` and storage-inventory tests — likely fixtures for archive state, fail-closed classification, interruption, and Linux/macOS reporting.

Maintainers may identify a narrower or different file set after choosing the owning surface.

## Non-goals

- Do not delete archives solely because they are old or large.
- Do not empty a user’s entire OS Trash.
- Do not weaken lock, CWD, owner, claim, identity, late-write, or native Git refusal protections.
- Do not automatically remove dirty, unique, unpushed, active, or unknown work.
- Do not introduce a generic home-directory cleaner.
- Do not require a new command if existing status/storage/maintenance surfaces can own the workflow cleanly.

## Suggested Validation Outcomes

- A synthetic steady workload demonstrates archive storage converges under the selected policy while protected archives survive.
- Fixtures cover clean merged archives, unpushed commits, tracked/untracked changes, unique ignored files, active tasks/sessions, incomplete metadata, duplicates, and identity changes.
- Repeated read-only plans are explainable and idempotent when state is unchanged.
- A state change between plan and apply blocks that candidate without blocking safe reporting for the rest.
- Linux and macOS fixtures reach equivalent safety decisions while using the intended platform/storage semantics.
- Existing archive-first integrity and interruption tests from #28822 continue to pass.

## Workarounds Applied

- Manually performed a read-only audit of 348 archived worktrees across both Trash locations.
- Froze a manifest to avoid chasing archives created by concurrent sessions.
- Classified conservatively and preserved 21 retain/unknown items.
- Avoided “Empty Trash” and all deletion because the available system action was too broad and did not cover both locations consistently.
- Saved a durable checkpoint and prepared targeted cleanup only after issue filing.

## Environment

- **aidevops version**: 3.32.216
- **Latest version**: 3.32.216
- **AI Assistant**: OpenCode
- **OS**: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
- **Shell**: bash 5.2.21
- **gh CLI**: 2.96.0

## Duplicate and Architectural Checks

- #28123 is the completed parent architecture; this issue reports a focused producer/lifecycle gap observed after that work.
- #22417 addressed safe permanent cleanup but predates the stronger archive-before-remove implementation.
- #28822 intentionally established the current recovery producer and safety boundary.
- #28860 addressed bounded TODO-sync temporary workspace cleanup, not retained registered-worktree recovery buckets.
- Searches for worktree archive retention, warning, storage, and cleanup found no open issue covering this focused operator lifecycle.

## Tier Rationale

`tier:thinking`: this is a design decision around destructive safety, operator consent, storage convergence, concurrency, and platform ownership. It should be decomposed only after maintainers choose the producer contract and operator surface.
